direct_answer: Painful hands can make cutting food and lifting cups difficult, and frailty can make meals slow and tiring. Adapted cutlery, good positioning and time help. Coughing, choking or a wet voice when eating may be signs of a swallowing problem and should be checked.

content:
Eating well matters for strength. When hands are painful and energy is low, meals can become hard work.

This guide covers practical ways to make meal times easier and safer. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Making eating easier

  • Cutlery with thick, light handles.
  • Plate guards or lipped plates.
  • Lightweight cups with two handles or lids.
  • Non-slip mats.
  • Pre-cut food or softer textures if chewing is tiring.

Positioning and time

  • Sit upright in a supportive chair, not slumped.
  • Allow plenty of time and avoid rushing.
  • Smaller, more frequent meals may be easier.
  • Stay upright for a while after eating.

Signs of swallowing problems

Coughing or choking when eating or drinking, a wet or gurgly voice after swallowing, food sticking, or repeated chest infections can be signs of dysphagia. See your GP, who may refer you to a speech and language therapist.

Help available

An occupational therapist can advise on equipment. A dietitian can help if you are losing weight. In care homes, staff should support meal times with dignity.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if someone is choking and cannot breathe, cough or speak.
  • Contact your GP or NHS 111 if swallowing problems are new or getting worse, or there are signs of a chest infection.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Who checks swallowing?

Speech and language therapists.

Where can I get adapted cutlery?

An OT can advise, and items are available from equipment suppliers.

Sources and further reading
